title: Columbus's First $500M Bond Project: 23 Affordable East Side Condos

body:
Columbus and the Central Ohio Community Land Trust broke ground August 27 on 23 income-restricted condos at East Broad Street and South Gould Road, the first project funded by the city's $500 million Affordable Housing Bond. The homes will sell for roughly $199,000 to buyers earning up to 120 percent of the area median income.

The city broke ground on the project August 27, a Thursday, at the corner of East Broad Street and South Gould Road, where a vacant lot will become 23 two- and three-bedroom condominiums. The developers plan to welcome homebuyers in fall 2027.

## What 'permanently affordable' actually means here

The Broad and Gould Condominiums use a community land trust structure, which is meaningfully different from how most affordable housing programs work. In a conventional affordable housing deal, affordability restrictions eventually expire and the price cap goes away. A community land trust prevents that outcome by severing ownership of the land from ownership of the building.

Under the [Central Ohio Community Land Trust](https://www.coclt.org/) model, COCLT retains ownership of the land beneath the building in perpetuity. Buyers purchase their individual condominium units and hold a 99-year ground lease on the underlying land rather than owning the land outright. When a homeowner sells, the next buyer must also be income-qualified, so the home stays affordable through every subsequent sale, not just the first.

## The bond funding

Columbus voters approved a $500 million Affordable Housing Bond in November 2025, [the largest local housing investment in city history](https://www.columbus.gov/Services/Housing-Assistance-Programs/Housing-Programs/Affordable-Housing-Bond-Investments), as part of a broader $1.9 billion bond package, [WOSU Public Media reported](https://www.wosu.org/politics-government/2026-02-11/columbus-leaders-lay-out-plans-for-500-million-affordable-housing-bond-package).

Mayor Andrew Ginther's administration laid out how the money would be spent at a February 2026 event: $125 million for shelter-system improvements and preserving existing affordable housing, $175 million for acquiring land and building denser housing, $150 million for building and preserving affordable rental units, and $50 million for reducing development costs through public-private partnerships, according to WOSU's reporting on the event.

The Broad and Gould project draws on that bond through direct city funding: Columbus is putting $3 million in Affordable Housing Bond money toward construction and another $1.1 million toward homebuyer assistance, [according to CW Columbus](https://cwcolumbus.com/news/local/home-affordability-crisis-continues-as-city-announces-199k-condos-coming-to-the-east-side) and [ABC6 On Your Side](https://abc6onyourside.com/news/local/home-affordability-crisis-continues-as-city-announces-199k-condos-coming-to-the-east-side).

Finance Fund is a third partner in the project, alongside the City of Columbus and COCLT.

## Who qualifies, and what buyers get

To purchase a Broad and Gould condo, buyers must earn no more than 120 percent of the Columbus area median income and complete COCLT's homebuyer orientation requirements. Curtiss Williams, president and CEO of the land trust's parent organization, told ABC6 that a single person typically needs to earn up to about $79,000 to qualify, and a family of four needs about $110,000.

At roughly $199,000, the condos price far below the broader Columbus market: the [July 2026 Columbus REALTORS report](https://columbusrealestatenews.com/blog/columbus-july-home-sales-climb-6-as-inventory-hits-decade-high) put the regional median sale price at $350,000, up 2.3 percent year-over-year, giving qualifying buyers a lower-cost entry point into homeownership.

## East Side context

The building will sit at East Broad Street and South Gould Road. East Broad is one of Columbus's major east-west arterials, running from downtown toward Bexley and beyond. The corridor has seen scattered new investment in recent years but no large-scale wave of market-rate condo development, which is part of why a $199,000 for-sale price point is viable here in a way it would not be in Short North or German Village.

## What to watch next

The immediate milestone is construction progress toward the fall 2027 completion date. Once units are ready, COCLT will run its usual homebuyer selection drawing; eligibility details are posted at [coclt.org](https://www.coclt.org/).

Longer term, Broad and Gould is an early test of how the city's housing bond performs at the neighborhood scale, at a moment when Columbus is trying to expand affordable homeownership beyond rental subsidies.

For more on East Side development, see CREN's [development coverage](https://columbusrealestatenews.com/topics/development).
